title: Loved by Allah and by people
word: Loved by Allah and by people
hookLine: renounce the world and Allah loves you, renounce what people have and they love you
tomorrow: someone hurts you first. are you allowed to hurt them back?

cards: A friend who never asks for anything is strangely easy to love. The one who always needs a ride, a charger, a favor, gets loved too, just more tiredly. So, yesterday's question.

A man comes to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and asks for a deed that will make Allah love him and people love him. The answer, in paraphrase from Ibn Majah's collection: renounce the world, and Allah will love you.
Renounce what people have, and people will love you.

teach.b: The word under it is zuhd: wanting little, letting go. The second half is plain enough: stop eyeing what other people have, and they relax around you. The first half is where two views live inside the tradition.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: LET GO IN THE HANDS.
teach.b: One view: zuhd means really letting go, in the hands. Own little, eat simply, keep the world at arm's length. Tradition tells of people who walked away from wealth for this.
Their best case: what you hold ends up holding you. Full hands can't reach for anything else.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: LET GO IN THE HEART.
teach.b: The other view: zuhd lives in the heart, not the hands. Ibn Rajab, writing on this very hadith, reports that Imam Ahmad was asked whether someone with a lot of money could still have zuhd.
He said yes, if he doesn't rejoice when it grows or grieve when it shrinks. Their best case: empty hands can hide a very busy heart, and wealth can be held loosely and given away.
Both views agree on more than they fight about.
The world isn't the enemy; the grip is.
And here's the line to tell a friend tonight: in this hadith, being loved by people comes from what you don't want from them.

how: Muslim teachers explain zuhd in different ways: some stress simple living and owning little, others stress a heart that holds wealth loosely; both warn against coveting what others have.

games.q: what does “loved by allah and by people” mean?
o: loved for letting go, by Allah and by others
liked for giving people all that they ask
admired for praying more than other people

p: no joy at gain, no grief at loss

s: zuhd means owning nothing; anyone with money can't have it
that's one view. Imam Ahmad said someone with wealth can, if the heart doesn't cling to it.
in this hadith, people's love comes from not wanting what they have
renounce what people have, and people will love you.
the two views on zuhd agree on nothing
both say the world isn't the enemy; the grip is.

games.q: your cousin says zuhd means owning almost nothing. you lean toward 'it's in the heart.' to be fair, what's her best case?
o: what you hold ends up holding you; letting go in the hands trains the heart.
she just doesn't like nice things, so she made it a rule.
the hadith says owning things is forbidden for believers.
games.why: the hands-first view's real argument: full hands can't reach for anything else. the heart-first view answers that empty hands can hide a busy heart. both live inside the tradition.

practice: Count on your fingers what you already have today that you didn't need to ask anyone for: this breath, a hand that works, water nearby, a place to sit. With each finger, notice the small ease of not needing one more thing.
When you run out of fingers, start the count again.

wordCard.voice: Loved by Allah and by people: the two loves in hadith thirty-one, one from letting go of the world, one from letting go of what others have.

orig.note: Arabic: renounce the world, and Allah will love you. izhad comes from the same root as zuhd.

carryVoice: Keep this one: want less, be loved, and loosen the grip on what's yours and what's theirs. That's hadith thirty-one.

sources.ref: Sunan Ibn Majah 4102 (Sahl ibn Sa'd: renounce the world and Allah will love you)
Ibn Rajab, Jami' al-'Ulum wa al-Hikam, on hadith 31 (Imam Ahmad on wealth and zuhd)
